world.title: AMECEA PLENARY: IMBISA Prays for Wisdom Ahead of AMECEA Leadership Elections
world.description:
By: Ginaba Lino
The Inter-Regional Meeting of the Bishops of Southern Africa (IMBISA) has assured the Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa (AMECEA) of its prayers and solidarity as the regional Catholic body elects new office-bearers and appoints new staff during its 21st Plenary Assembly.
In a goodwill message read during the plenary assembly in Nairobi, Kenya, on behalf of the IMBISA President, Archbishop Liborius Ndumbukuti Nashenda, the region prayed for divine wisdom to guide the election of new leaders who will steer AMECEA's mission in the years ahead.
“May God give you wisdom as you elect new officer-bearers and appoint new staff members for AMECEA. We assure you of our prayers as they take up their task of building bridges of communion, hope, justice and good governance,” Fr. Enrico Parry said on behalf of the President.
In his message, the Southern African bishops also congratulated AMECEA on its 65th anniversary, describing the milestone as a testament to decades of collegial collaboration among the bishops of the region.
“With thanksgiving before the Lord who gathers us in His Church, we celebrate your 65th year of existence. We pray that the collegial experience of the years past may now bear rich and abundant fruit in the growth of synodality in your region.”
Reaffirming the close relationship between the two regional episcopal bodies, Fr. Parry expressed solidarity with the bishops as they deliberate on strengthening the Church's engagement with young people.
“We stand with you, our dear brothers in the episcopate, as you reflect on the synodal journey with young people: building bridges of communion, hope, justice and good governance,” he said.
Archbishop Nashenda emphasized that although AMECEA has consistently placed young people at the center of its pastoral priorities, the current assembly offers a renewed opportunity for the Church to embrace the guidance of the Holy Spirit in responding to the aspirations of a new generation.
He prayed that the enthusiasm, creativity and energy of young people would inspire the bishops in their discussions and decision-making.
“May the vitality and energy God gives to young people be yours, too, in your reflections and deliberations.”
Archbishop Nashenda expressed hope that the outcomes of the plenary assembly would strengthen the Church's witness beyond Eastern Africa.
May your work at this plenary session show the way forward for the Church in Africa,” he said, before offering his fraternal greetings in Christ on behalf of IMBISA.
The assembly is expected to conclude on Sunday with Holy Mass celebration presided over by the new AMECEA New Chairman (Votive Mass for AMECEA Family of God), announcement of new office Bearers, and communique to close the 21st Plenary assembly.
world.source: Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa

world.title: AMECEA PLENARY: TEC President Urges Clergy to Bridge the Gap, Young People to Explore Opportunities
world.description:
By Dalphina Rubyema
Although the President of the Tanzania Episcopal Conference (TEC) acknowledged that the 21st Plenary Assembly of the Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa (AMECEA) has been exceptional in bringing youth issues to the forefront, he emphasized that the challenges facing young people cannot be solved overnight.
Instead, Rt. Rev. Wolfgang Pisa said, the Church must intentionally build bridges that bring Church leaders and young people together to identify and develop opportunities available within their communities. He made these comments in an interview during the 21st AMECEA Plenary Assembly, currently taking place at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA) in Nairobi, Kenya.
“The 21st Plenary Assembly, which also coincided with the 65th anniversary of AMECEA, has been unique because of its deliberate focus on young people and the challenges they face,” the member of the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin (OFM Cap) said, describing the assembly as an invitation for the Church to continue accompanying and walking with young people as they seek lasting solutions to their difficulties.
Bishop Pisa of the Catholic Diocese of Lindi, Tanzania, said the assembly is also unique because of highlighting issues affecting young people in the Church, society, and the World.
He explained that a wide range of youth-related challenges were presented, many of them directly by young people themselves and supported by research and statistical evidence from experts. The AMECEA bishops, he noted, were presented with data showing that young people constitute between 25 and 50 percent of the Catholic population in member countries.
The Assembly also observed that, despite their significant numbers, many young people have not been adequately involved in pastoral planning and decision-making, although Bishop Pisa noted that the Church has already established structures to engage them.
He pointed to Tanzania as an example, where the Church has age-specific pastoral groups, including the Holy Childhood Association for primary school children, the Tanzania Youth Catholic Students (TYCS) for secondary school students, the Tanzania Catholic University Students (TMCS) for students in institutions of higher learning, and Young Catholic Workers (VIWAWA) for youth who have employment.
“Young people have not been forgotten. Most countries have developed institutional structures through which they are accompanied according to their stage of life,” he reiterated.
However, Bishop Pisa stressed that more youth-friendly structures are still needed to keep young people actively engaged in the life and mission of the Church. Among these, he said, is giving them greater opportunities to participate in Church leadership.
At the same time, he challenged young people to demonstrate responsibility and integrity whenever they are entrusted with leadership positions. Bishop Pisa added that “Many young people are still in a stage of searching for their future and striving to establish themselves in life. When they are given positions of responsibility within the Church, they must prove themselves trustworthy and accountable,” he said.
He emphasized that excluding young people from leadership weakens the Church itself. “Young people are an essential part of the Church. Failing to involve them fully is equivalent to weakening the Church.”
Responding to concerns raised by young delegates about the lack of close relationships between young people and the clergy, Bishop Pisa said the issue requires deliberate action to build stronger connections between the two groups. He encouraged priests to overcome the distance that sometimes exists due to busy pastoral schedules and to invest more intentionally in accompanying young people.
“Young people are the Church of today and the Church of tomorrow. Strengthening the relationship between them and the clergy requires serious reflection. Youth chaplains, in particular, must fully embrace their mission. There is clearly a gap, which is why young people have expressed the feeling that they have no place. Being a chaplain is not merely a title; it is a ministry that requires understanding how to respond to the needs of today's young people,” he said.
Bishop Pisa also expressed concern that some politicians exploit the economic hardships faced by young people to advance their personal or political interests. He said that once these politicians have served their purpose, many are abandoned without any meaningful support or opportunities to improve their lives, leaving some struggling with frustration and mental stress.
According to the TEC President, preventing young people from feeling compelled to migrate abroad in search of better opportunities requires a joint effort by the Church and society to accompany them and help them recognize and utilize the opportunities available within their own communities.
“We cannot claim that we will solve all the challenges facing young people overnight. However, if we remain close to them, we can help them discover the opportunities that exist in their own environment and accompany them so that they can benefit from those opportunities,” he emphasized.
world.source: Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa

world.title: AMECEA PLENARY: AMECEA’s 21st Plenary Seeks to Reconnect Young People with the Church
world.description:
By Luke Bisani
The Bishop of the Catholic Diocese of Embu in Kenya, Rt. Rev. Peter Kimani, has commended the 21st Plenary of the Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa (AMECEA) for focusing on the challenges facing young people and seeking ways to strengthen their relationship with the Church.
“Young people today are grappling with numerous challenges, including social and economic difficulties, as well as conflicting messages and teachings that can affect their faith and sense of belonging.” Bishop Kimani, who also serves as Vice-Chairman of the Commission for Youth Apostolate at the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB), urged young people after the business session of the 21st Plenary on Thursday.
Bishop Kimani added that the Plenary has provided young people with an opportunity to express themselves and share their experiences, adding that the responsibility now rests with Church leaders to respond to their concerns and translate their recommendations into concrete action.
The youths, on their part, have noted that it is now their role to be proactive and respond to the recommendations and be part of the Church, Bishop Kimani reiterated.
He said the Plenary has been designed to help reconnect young people with the Church by listening to their voices and creating a Church and society where they feel welcomed, valued and included.
The Bishop further noted that the Church must also find innovative ways to reach young people in the digital spaces where they spend much of their time, describing the digital environment as an important pastoral space for evangelization and engagement.
Bishop Kimani urged Church leaders to view the re-energizing of young people's faith as a pastoral opportunity that requires greater involvement, collaboration and partnership between young people and pastoral leaders.
He acknowledged that empowering young people to actively participate in the life and mission of the Church would strengthen their faith and enable them to contribute meaningfully to their communities' development.
world.source: Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa

world.title: AMECEA PLENARY: Bishop Assures Eastern Africa Church of Return to Normalcy in South Sudan’s Wau Diocese
world.description:
Janet Wambui Hinga
The Catholic Diocese of Wau in South Sudan is steadily returning to normalcy following years of civil conflict, with previously abandoned parishes reopening and communities gradually returning to their homes, Bishop Matthew Remijio has said.
Speaking during an interview at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA) in Nairobi, where while attending the 21st AMECEA Plenary Assembly, the South Sudanese prelate acknowledged that improved security and strong collaboration between the Church and the government have enabled pastoral work to resume across much of the diocese.
Wau Diocese is very vast, and we are enjoying the pastoral work there because there is stability, the bishop said. I thank the government for that because you can move day and night freely. In the diocese, there is security that allows the bishop to carry out his pastoral work freely.
The bishop further explained that restoring the Church's presence in communities affected by war became one of his priorities after assuming leadership of the diocese.
The first thing I did was undertake pastoral visits to all the parishes. I took the risk and courage to reopen all the parishes that had been suspended during the war because I believe that the presence of a priest in any place brings people back. The priest is there for them.
Although the diocese has made significant progress, His Lordship acknowledged both the challenges and the joys of pastoral ministry, saying they continue to shape the day-to-day mission of the Church.
The Catholic Diocese of Wau is very vast. It has more than 3.6 million Catholics. Despite all the challenges, the long distances and poor roads for pastoral work, once you reach the people, you forget all the pain, the suffering, and the rough roads because you receive a warm welcome. The people are attentive, receptive, and eager to listen.
Among the key priorities of the youthful bishop is the use of communication as an essential tool for evangelization. He highlighted the diocesan radio station, Voice of Hope, as a trusted source of information for both the Church and civil authorities.
This is a vital radio station. People across the states are listening to it because it is reliable. Even the government, when they want to reach the citizens, comes to the Church radio because it reaches Rumbek, Juba, and four states. It makes communication much easier.
Despite the progress made in the diocese, Bishop Remijio appealed for continued support from the global Church and people of goodwill for a diocese whose needs range from infrastructure and pastoral facilities to professional expertise in education, healthcare, and administration.
We need everything, he said. Not only financial support, but also experts who can help us strengthen our institutions, our schools, hospitals, and pastoral work.
While Wau currently enjoys relative stability, the bishop acknowledged that insecurity persists in other parts of South Sudan, disrupting pastoral activities and displacing communities.
He reaffirmed the Catholic Church's commitment to promoting peace, reconciliation, and national unity through dialogue and prophetic witness.
The Church will never stop advocating for peace and reconciliation, he said. Our mission is to encourage peaceful coexistence among all the sons and daughters of South Sudan.
Reflecting on the steps being taken by the Church in Eastern Africa to address the challenges facing young people across the region, Bishop Remijio expressed hope regarding the active participation of the youth in the synodal journey.
From what I have seen through the participation of the youth in this Synod, there is hope. There is hope for the youth in East Africa, especially in their active role in the Church and society. The message I can give them is that despite the challenging economic situation and all they are going through as they struggle to find their place in the Church and society, they should not give up.
He added that the call by young people for greater inclusion in decision-making, a recurring theme during the assembly, would be embraced through discernment in keeping with the mind of the Mother Church and within the synodal journey.
We have opened this opportunity for them to participate fully with us in the decision-making process in the Church and in society. In the Church, all forums are now open for young people to participate actively. Before making any decision, we have to discern together according to the mind of the Mother Church, and together we reach the decision-making stage.
They should not give up because the Church depends on them, society depends on them, and tomorrow the Church will continue to depend on them, he urged.
world.source: Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa

science.title: Unwritten social rules, not government oversight, help keep forest land sustainable
science.description: Swidden agriculture—often called "slash-and-burn"—has been practiced on every inhabited continent throughout human history, and for decades it has been blamed for the destruction of the world's rainforests. However, a new study of more than 18,000 forest patches around the world found that the environmental impact of swidden is more nuanced and less destructive than the term "slash-and-burn" suggests—and that unwritten social rules in small societies, not government oversight, often regulate land use closely enough to support both harvests and forest regeneration sustainably over time.
